897.howItsDone: Hindu art and temple images show Krishna holding a flute, and devotees sing songs about it at home and in temples; the Bhagavata's chapter on the flute is read aloud and sung in devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Govardhan lifted. The storm came down on the village, and a boy held up a hill so everyone could shelter underneath.

A calf is drinking from its mother, and it stops. The milk is still in its mouth. It doesn't swallow. It just stands there, ears up. Somewhere past the pasture, among the trees, someone is playing a flute. That calf comes from the Bhagavata Purana, from a chapter where the women of Vraja, the gopis, stay behind in the village while Krishna takes the cows to the forest. They can't see him. They can only hear him. So they tell each other what the sound is doing to everything it reaches.
screen: `A CALF FORGETS TO SWALLOW.` → `A FLUTE IN THE TREES.` → `THE GOPIS CAN ONLY HEAR.`

segments.voice: In this chapter Krishna doesn't teach anyone. He just plays, walking into the autumn forest with his brother Balarama and the herd. The gopis fill in the picture from memory: a peacock feather in his hair, flowers at his ears, a yellow cloth, a garland of forest flowers, his lips on the bamboo. Then they turn to the listeners, and that list is the heart of the chapter. The cows lift their ears and drink in the sound; the calves stand with milk in their mouths. The birds settle on the branches and close their eyes. The does of the forest gaze at him, their mates beside them. The rivers, the gopis say, slow their current and reach out with their waves to hold his feet and offer him lotuses. Even the clouds, seeing him walk in the heat, drift over him to give him shade. Look at the audience. Not priests, not kings: cows, birds, deer, water, weather. Whatever hears the music stops what it was doing. And the gopis? At home, at their work, talking. The sound reaches them and he doesn't, so their delight and their ache come from the same place. Some devotional readers hear the whole world turned into a listener here, every creature called at once. Others hear a village falling in love with a sound. Either way, the chapter never explains the flute. It just shows what it does, down to a calf that forgets to swallow.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the flute. The calves stood with milk in their mouths, the birds closed their eyes, and the rivers slowed.

What did a stick do to deserve this? That's the gopis' question, and they're not joking. They're still in the village, still listening, and one of them says what the others are thinking. Krishna's lips are on that flute all day. It's a length of bamboo cut from some riverbank, with no voice of its own, no family, no story. And it gets closer to him than any of them. So they ask, half in envy and half in wonder: what good thing did this flute ever do?
screen: `WHAT DID A STICK DO?` → `CLOSER TO HIM THAN ANY OF THEM.` → `FROM THE SIDE OF THE FLUTE.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata gives the question to one gopi. What virtue did this flute practice, she asks, that it enjoys the sweetness of his lips, a sweetness the gopis feel is theirs, and leaves them only what's left over? Then she answers herself, in a strange and lovely way. She looks at the bamboo's family. The lakes and rivers whose water raised it are glad: their lotuses open like hair standing up on skin. And the trees, the bamboo's elders, let their sap run down like tears, the way old people weep with joy when someone in the family turns out devoted. So halfway through her sentence, envy turns into praise. Someone from the riverbank got close to Krishna, and the whole riverbank is proud. Now look at what a flute is. A hollow reed. Breath goes in one end and comes out as music; the flute adds nothing but the empty space. Some devotional teachers return to that detail: the flute is close to Krishna because there's nothing inside it in the way. They hear the gopi's question as the devotee's question, what would it take to be that close, and the flute as the answer: a life with room in it. That's an interpretation, not a line in the chapter. The chapter just leaves us with a woman in a village, jealous of a piece of bamboo, and then glad for it.
screen: `WHAT GOOD DID THIS FLUTE EVER DO?` · `THE RIVERS AND TREES ARE PROUD.` · `A HOLLOW REED, EMPTY INSIDE.` · then, large: `A LIFE WITH ROOM IN IT.`

segments.voice: Let your breath be the only thing moving through you, the way breath moves through a reed: in without grabbing, out without pushing. If you pray, you can offer that room to Krishna, or to God by any name you use.

screen: `THE FLUTE.` · `JEALOUS OF A REED, THEN GLAD.`

segments.voice: The milk is on the fire. Someone is halfway through milking a cow. Someone is serving food to her family. Someone has a baby at her breast. It's an autumn night in Vraja, the moon full and coming up red over the trees, and every house is in the middle of something. Then, from the forest, the flute. Not the daytime music the gopis talked about from a distance. This time, the Bhagavata says, the sound is calling them.
screen: `THE MILK IS ON THE FIRE.` → `A FULL MOON OVER THE TREES.` → `THIS TIME, THE FLUTE CALLS.`

segments.voice: The text slows down and goes house by house. The women hear the flute and go, each one exactly as she is. The one milking leaves the cow. The one boiling milk leaves the pot on the fire. The one cooking leaves the food unserved. The one feeding a child, the one waiting on her husband, the one eating her own dinner: all of them stand up and go. Some were dressing or putting on makeup, and they go with their clothes and ornaments in disarray. Husbands, fathers and brothers try to stop them; they don't turn around. And some, the Bhagavata adds, were kept inside, and those women shut their eyes and went to him in meditation instead. Why linger on the half-finished jobs? Because the list is the point. Nobody finishes anything, waits for a better time, or makes herself presentable first. Devotional readers hear a picture of the soul when God calls: it doesn't arrive polished, it arrives as it is, mid-task, with the milk still on the stove. And the Bhagavata doesn't let the scene pass unexamined. Right after this, the king who's listening stops the story to ask how a love like theirs could set anyone free, and Krishna himself will tell the women to go home. That's where tomorrow begins. Tonight, the scene is enough: a village full of unfinished things, and women on the road into the trees, running toward a sound.
screen: `EACH ONE GOES EXACTLY AS SHE IS.` · `SOME KEPT INSIDE GO IN MEDITATION.` · `NOBODY FINISHES ANYTHING FIRST.` · then, large: `MID-TASK, AS SHE IS.`

segments.voice: Notice what you just set down to be here, a phone, a cup, a list, and leave it untidied. 900.howItsDone: The rasa lila chapters of the Bhagavata are recited and sung by Krishna devotees and danced in the Ras Lila performances of Vrindavan and other places; teachers in the devotional traditions present them as a picture of the soul's love for God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the flute on the full-moon night. The gopis left the milk on the fire and the cow half milked, and went exactly as they were.

Before the dance, a king interrupts. In the Bhagavata, the sage Shuka is telling this story to King Parikshit, who has just heard about the women running into the forest at night. He stops the story. These women, he says, knew Krishna as a beloved, not as the highest truth. Their minds were full of him the way a lover's mind is full. How could that set them free? It's a fair question, and the text answers it before going one step further.
screen: `A KING INTERRUPTS.` → `THEY KNEW HIM AS A BELOVED.` → `HOW COULD THAT SET THEM FREE?`

segments.voice: Shuka's answer goes back to an earlier story: Shishupala, a king who hated Krishna, spent his life thinking of him in rage, and still reached him in the end. If hatred fixed on him could do that, Shuka says, then whoever turns the whole mind toward him, in desire or anger, fear, affection, kinship or friendship, becomes absorbed in him. What matters is where the mind is pointed. That's the frame. Only then does the story go on. The women arrive, out of breath, and Krishna greets them like a polite host. Then he tells them to go home. The night is dark, the forest full of animals, your families will be looking for you, your place is with them. It's a test, and it lands hard. The gopis stand with eyes down, scratching the ground with their toes, crying. Then they answer. Their hearts were taken by him, they say, and their feet won't carry them back. They came not for a household but for him. Krishna smiles, stays, and the night of play in the forest begins. It doesn't go smoothly for long. As he honors them, the women grow proud, each one sure she is the most favored woman in the world. At that moment, the text says, Krishna vanishes. Some devotional teachers read the whole episode as the soul's longing for God, told in the language of human love; Parikshit's question is the text's own reminder to read it that way.
screen: `WHERE THE MIND IS POINTED.` · `GO HOME, HE SAYS.` · `OUR FEET WON'T CARRY US BACK.` · then, large: `PRIDE, AND HE VANISHES.`

901.title: the rasa lila (with the Keeper's framing)
901.hook: the rasa lila (with the Keeper's framing)
901.howItsDone: Devotees recite and sing the Gopi Gita from the Bhagavata, and the circle dance with Krishna between every two gopis is painted, sung, and performed in Ras Lila dance dramas.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rasa lila began with a king's question and a frame. Whoever turns the whole mind toward Krishna is absorbed in him. Then pride, and he vanished.

Have you seen him? The gopis are asking the trees. They go from one to the next in the moonlit forest, a fig, a tulsi plant, a jasmine vine, asking whether he passed this way. Nobody answers. A moment ago they were sure they were the luckiest women alive. Now they're searching the forest floor for a footprint.
screen: `HAVE YOU SEEN HIM?` → `ASKING THE TREES.` → `THE SEARCH, THE SONG, THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: They do find footprints, his, and beside them a woman's. He has taken one gopi with him. But she grows proud too, asks him to carry her, and he vanishes from her as well. The others find her weeping alone, and now they're all in the same place: together, without him. So they go down to the bank of the Yamuna and sing. Tradition calls their song the Gopi Gita. It has a reproach or two, but mostly it's a long remembering, his walk, his flute, his face coming home with the cows at dusk, and running through it, the plain plea to show himself. Then he's there, smiling, a garland around his neck. The gopis ask him a riddle about love: some love those who love them, some love those who don't, some love nobody. Which is he? Krishna answers that he stepped away so their love would deepen, the way a poor man who finds treasure and loses it thinks of nothing else. Then the one they worship says something startling: he can't repay them. Their own goodness will have to be their reward. Only then does the dance itself happen, the rasa. The women form a circle, and Krishna appears between every two of them, so each one feels him at her side. The Bhagavata closes with one more frame for the listener: whoever hears this with faith gains devotion and is freed from the craving that troubles the heart. A story this full of longing calls itself medicine for craving.

902.title: leaving Vrindavan
902.howItsDone: Akrura is remembered by devotees as a model of longing to see God; the chapters of his journey to Vraja are recited from the Bhagavata, and pilgrims to the Vrindavan area visit places linked with the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rasa lila ended. The search, the song by the river, and the circle, with Krishna between every two gopis.

A chariot is on the road to Vraja, and its driver is carrying a trap. King Kamsa of Mathura has learned that the cowherd boy everyone talks about is the son he was warned of, the one born to kill him. So Kamsa plans a festival: a contest of wrestlers, and an elephant at the gate. All he needs is someone the boys will trust to bring them. He chooses Akrura, a respected elder of their own clan. Akrura agrees to go.
screen: `A CHARIOT CARRYING A TRAP.` → `KAMSA NEEDS A MESSENGER.` → `AKRURA AGREES TO GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the surprise. Akrura is Kamsa's messenger, and Krishna's devotee. The Bhagavata spends the whole ride inside his head, and what's there isn't dread. It's longing. All the way he turns one thought over: I'm going to see him. Will Krishna look at him kindly, or hold him at arm's length as the king's man? He counts the long errand as good fortune, because of where it ends. He reaches Vraja at sunset, as the cows come home. In the dust of the cow pen he sees footprints, and knows whose they are; the text says they carry the marks devotees look for on the soles of Krishna's feet. Akrura jumps down from his chariot and rolls in that dust, overcome. Then Krishna and Balarama come out to meet him. No arm's length. The brothers embrace him, take his hand, lead him in, wash his feet and feed him. Krishna asks after his family, and only then asks what brought him. And Akrura, the king's messenger, tells them everything: Kamsa's hatred, the festival, the plan. Krishna and Balarama laugh, and agree to go. Two loyalties ride in that chariot, and the story doesn't scold him for either. It lets us watch a man doing a hard errand with his heart pointed somewhere else.

903.title: leaving Vrindavan
903.howItsDone: The gopis' grief at Krishna's departure is a theme of devotional poetry and song, and devotees in the Vrindavan area remember the place associated with his leaving.

segments.voice: Yesterday: leaving Vrindavan began on the road. Akrura, the king's messenger, rode toward Vraja full of longing, and rolled in the dust of Krishna's footprints.

The news gets around the village overnight. By morning everyone knows: Akrura has come from Mathura, and he's taking Krishna and Balarama with him. The cowherd men load carts with pots of milk and butter as gifts for the king. And the gopis, who ran into the forest at the sound of a flute, stand in the road beside the chariot. This time there's nothing to run toward.
screen: `THE NEWS GETS AROUND OVERNIGHT.` → `CARTS LOADED FOR MATHURA.` → `THE ONES WHO STAY.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata gives the gopis a long, raw lament, and doesn't tidy it up. They blame the creator, who brings people together and pulls them apart for no reason, like a child playing and spoiling the game. They turn on Akrura too. His name means not cruel, they say, and it doesn't fit: he's come to carry off the one thing they have. They imagine the women of Mathura, who will see Krishna every day now, and wonder whether a city boy will remember village girls. Then they stop caring what anyone thinks, and cry out his names in the road. The chariot moves. Krishna sees them and sends back word through a messenger, as the text puts it: I will come back. And the gopis stand watching until the flag on the chariot and the dust behind it are gone. Look at the shape of this week. A flute that stopped the cows in the pasture. A gopi jealous of a hollow reed. A full-moon night with the milk left on the fire, and the frame: where the whole mind is turned. The search, the song, the circle with Krishna beside every one. And now the same women in the road, with the same longing, and nowhere to go. The Bhagavata doesn't treat the parting as the end of their love. Some devotional teachers say it's where that love is tested most deeply, in remembering him from a distance. The story will come back to these women.
screen: `THEY BLAME THE CREATOR, AND AKRURA.` · `I WILL COME BACK.` · `UNTIL THE DUST IS GONE.` · then, large: `A WEEK OF LONGING.`
